In Brahms's Fourth Symphony, much that is attractive – most of it, however, was unsatisfactory.” — The entries for March 19 and 23 are written as a single entry.
28. Jupiter-Sinfonie 1. u. 2. Satz 4-händig.
30. Gespräch über Peter,Probably the children’s nursery rhyme Das Kleine Peter Liedchen (see lesson notes for October 25). sie bittet um Rat.
2. IV. Händel 1. u. 2. Stück wiederholt u. abgesetzt.
4. Bild zu Brahms Capriccio neu, korrigiert; wiederholen den 1. Satz der Jupiter-Sinfonie, sie primo.

6. Haydn Sinfonie Ddur No 10 ganz durchgegangen (zum Furtwängler-Konzert); Eroica 1. Satz.On April 7, 1929, Furtwängler conducted the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra in a concert that included Haydn’s Symphony No. 86 in D major and Beethoven’s “Eroica.”

9. Beide Stücke in Partitur durchgegangen, dazu Furtwänglers Vortrag.The pieces in question are Haydn’s Symphony No. 86 in D major and Beethoven’s “Eroica,” which Furtwängler conducted in a concert of the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra on April 7, 1929.
11. Brünauers auswendig geschriebenes Händel-Allegro durchgegangen.Cf. Brünauer’s lesson for April 4: “He brings the Handel Allegro written from memory, really good.”

13. Ueber Furtwänglers IX.;This remark, found also in Albersheim’s lesson notes, may refer to a recollection of a performance of the Ninth Symphony by Furtwängler, or to the conductor’s remarks about his approach to the work. A live performance or broadcast of the work in Vienna in early 1929 is not recorded. zu Brahms Capriccio Fingersatz u. Vortrag neu.
16. Brahms Capriccio gespielt.
18. Mittelteil des Capriccio begonnen.

20. Korrekturen von E. Bachs Fermatebilder;C. P. E. Bach, Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Eng. transl. William J. Mitchell (New York: W. W. Norton; London: Cassell, 1949; London: Eulenburg, 1974), pp. 384–86 “The Fermata” (= chapter XXXI). zeige die von mir ausgearbeitete Fermate.
25. Korrektur zu Brahms Bildern abgeschlossen.
27. Spielt das Adagio aus Em. Bachs Sonate.
30. Fingersatz zum Mittelteil in Brahms Capriccio.

2. V. Noch einmal Haydns Sinfonie Ddur, in der Partitur die bemerkenswertesten Stellen durchgegangen; vierhändig den 1. Satz gespielt, sie primo.Diary May 2: “During Miss Elias's lesson, the Graf Zeppelin appears over Vienna!”
4. Aus Haydns Sinfonie vierhändig den 2. Satz gespielt, sie primo. Trägt in ihre Partitur Notizen ein.
9. Haydns Sinfonie abgeschlossen.
11. Zeige eigene Bilder zu Brahms Rhapsodie Hmoll.
14. Rundfunk-Bemerkungen; Brahms Capriccio ganz gespielt.
16. Stellen aus der Eroica Durchführung; ich korrigire die Hintergrundbilder zu der von mir ausgearbeiteten Fermate.
18. Em. Bach Sonate, letzter Satz gespielt, Erläuterung flüchtig.

21. Ueber Toscanini! Ich bringe unermüdlich zu Bewußtsein, daß ich ähnlich festgelegtes Spiel seit jeher von meinen Schülern fordere, es aber weder bei den Jungen im Berufe, noch bei den Liebhabern durchsetzen konnte: es verlangt Not, stete Kontrolle, unausgesetzte Pflege. In diesem Linie sei Spiel mehr als das Schreiben von Bildern, das nur einmalig ist. Historisches zu Donizetti: Der Baß kontrapunktiert nicht – u. Musik ist von Anfang an ein Außensatz gewesen.
26. Beethoven op. 14I, 1. Satz begonnen.
1. VI. Beethoven op. 14I, 1. Satz zuende.

6. Brahms IV.
1. u. 4. Satz vierhändig gespielt, einmal sie, einmal ich primo.
8. Beethoven op. 14I, 2. u. 3. Satz abgeschlossen.
13. Brahms Liebeslieder Walzer, vierhändig mit methodischer Vortragsanweisung, sie primo.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Angi Elias in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: October 2: Brahms Op. 76, No. 7, in A minor, new.
October 4: Schenker Op. 4, No. 1, graph corrected; graphs by Hahn, Hamburg, shown to her.
October 6: Beethoven, Op. 10, No. 3, third movement, new, read; the voice-leading line shown to her in passing.
October 11: Graphs for Brahms and Schenker improved.

October 13: Brahms String Quartet in A minor, the Andante played four-hands, in part
the voice-leading line also shown to her; a few things about the “Eroica”.
October 16: Brahms played.
October 18: p. 24 of Beethoven in accordance with Mikulitsch shown him.
October 20: Beethoven Op. 10, last movement, elucidated and played.
October 25: Little Peter’s Song corrected; I show her the Overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream.
October 27: On Casals’s performance; Chopin Nocturne in E major from Op. 9; on radio broadcasts.
October 30: First correction of Brahms’s Op. 76, No. 6.
November 3: Brahms Tragic Overture, four-hands, begun.
November 6: On Rosenthal’s performance of the “Hammerklavier” Sonata, Op. 106, and Chopin Prelude in D major.
November 10: Tragic Overture completed; on Hoesslin and the violin virtuoso Spalding.

November 13: On the performance of Brahms First Symphony
(Hoesslin); on Das Rheingold on the radio.
November 15: Observations on Tautenhayn’s “Schubert and his Time”; on dances by Beethoven, Lanner, etc.
November 17: On Schubert’s B minor Symphony and Berrsche’s thoughts; I show her the song “An den Mond” from the Peters edition, volume 7. Revisitations: Prelude in D major, Waltz in A major.
November 20: Remarks on the Schubert celebration; further thoughts on Chopin’s Waltz in A major. Fingering for Brahms’s Op. 76, No. 6.
November 22: Brahms played.
November 24: On Schubert’s operas. Revisitation: Waltz in C minor; Nocturne in E major from Op. 9, new.
November 27: On Furtwängler’s performance of Schubert’s C major Symphony; on the ornaments in the Prelude in D major; connection created by intensification (cf. Brünauer).
November 29: Rosamunde in Furtwängler’s performance.
December 1: Beethoven’s Op. 13, new.
December 4: Schubert Minuet in B minor, corrected in accordance with the facsimile.
December 6: Schubert, performance.
December 13: Rosenthal’s study of pedalling (in his edition of Liszt).
December 15: I show here Dunn’s Ornamentation; Haydn’s “Schoolmaster” Symphony in E major, Adagio.
December 20: On neighbor-note harmonies and my new signatures, examples of this from Beethoven’s Op. 10, No. 3: IV9-8. I show here Schoenberg’s article on octave doubling.
December 22: Op. 13, first movement completed; the Allegretto from Brahms’s String Quartet in C minor played four-hands; she brings presents.
December 27: Graph of the F major passage from the Andante of Schubert’s Symphony in C major.
December 29: Beethoven Op. 13, Adagio, performance primarily taken from my personal copy of the score.
January 3: The graph for the Schubert Symphony corrected and elucidated.
January 5:The graph of the Adagio from Op. 13 corrected; concerning some performances on the radio.

January 8: On Friedmann on the radio, especially his technique of emphasizing the weak
beats of a bar.
January 12: The performance markings entered into Beethoven’s Adagio.
January 15: About Christian? Bach and Goldsand; Schumann’s Piano Concerto.
January 17:I show her the facsimile of Chopin’s Op. 10, No. 12.
January 19: The Adagio from Op. 13 played.
January 22: Handel Suite No. 2, new; I correct the first graph and play to her.
January 24: On Beethoven’s Piano Concerto (Wang).
January 26: The Rondo of Op. 13 completed.
January 29: Fingering and performance for the first movement of the Handel.
January 31: Beethoven Concerto finished; Second Symphony (remarks on Spörr).
February 2: C. P. E. Bach’s Württemberg Sonatas, No. 4, new.
February 5: I show her Brünauer’s piece. On the graph of the introduction to Handel, the voice-leading gone over once again.

February 7: Hoboken’s march played four-hands; precise entry of the diminutions: fifths, sixths, neighbor-notes. The
trill in the graph of the first movement of Handel.
February 9: On the first movement of C. P. E. Bach: voice-leading line, fingering, performance.
February 19: Graphs for the introduction completed.
February 21: Notes on performance entered.
February 28: Graphs for the introduction completed.
March 2: Fermata studies according to C. P. E. Bach’s text and test pieces.
March 5: Fingering for the first part of the Allegro.
March 7: Correction of the second part.
March 9: Image of C. P. E. Bach’s fermata corrected.
March 12: Graphs of the Allegro completed, and so Handel put away for this year. New: the Capriccio in B minor from Brahms’s Op. 76.
March 14: Brahms Sonata Op. 99 for Cello and Piano: a passage in the development section (Casals).
March 16: Brahms’s Fourth Symphony, first movement played four-hands, a few things about the voice-leading line.
March 19: On Furtwängler’s performance of the “Jupiter” Symphony and Brahms’s Fourth Symphony.
March 23: On Furtwängler’s performance of the “Jupiter” Symphony and Brahms’s Fourth Symphony.
March 28: “Jupiter” Symphony, first and second movements played four-hands.
March 30: Conversation about Peter, she asks for advice.
April 2: Handel, first and second movement repeated and set aside.
April 4: Graph of Brahms’s Capriccio, new, corrected; we revisit the first movement of the “Jupiter” Symphony, she taking the upper part.
April 9: Both pieces studied in full score, also Furtwängler’s performance.
April 11: The graph of Handel’s Allegro, written out from memory by Brünauer, studied carefully.
April 13: On Furtwänglers Ninth; on Brahms’s Capriccio, fingering and performance new.
April 16: Brahms’s Capriccio played.
April 18: Middle section of the Capriccio begun.
April 20: Corrections to the graphs of C. P. E. Bach’s fermatas; I show her the fermata elaborated by me.
April 25: Corrections to the graphs of the Brahms completed.
April 27: She plays the Adagio from C. P. E. Bach’s Sonata.
April 30: Fingering for the middle section of Brahms’s Capriccio.
May 2: Once again Haydn’s Symphony in D major, the most noteworthy passages in the score studied carefully; the first movement played four-hands, she on the upper part.
May 4: The second movement of Haydn’s Symphony played four-hands, she on the upper part. She enters notes into her score.
May 9: Haydn’s Symphony completed.
May 11: I show her my own graphs to Brahms’s Rhapsody in B minor.
May 14: Remarks about the radio; Brahms’s Capriccio played in its entirety.
May 16: Passages from the development section of the Eroica; I correct the background graphs to the fermatas by C. P. E. Bach that I elaborated.
May 18: C. P. E. Bach Sonata, last movement played; elucidation given hastily.

May 21: Concerning Toscanini! I relentlessly make my students aware that I have always demanded of them a similarly secure playing technique, but neither the young professionals nor the amateurs can follow through on this; it requires necessity, constant control, constant attention. In this sense, playing is more than the writing-out of graphs, which is merely a single act. Historical assessment of Donizetti: his bass lines do not contribute to the counterpoint – and music has from the outset been a counterpoint between the outer voices.
May 26: Beethoven Op. 14, No. 1, first movement begun.
May 28: Performance study for Brahms’s Capriccio, on the basis of Brahms’s instructions; the piece is played.
June 1: Beethoven Op. 14, No. 1, first movement completed.

June 6: Brahms’s Fourth Symphony,
first and fourth movements played four-hands, once she, once I taking the upper part.
June 8: Beethoven Op. 14, No. 1, second and third movements completed.
June 13: Brahms’s Liebeslieder waltzes, played four-hands with methodical instruction on performance, she taking the upper part.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Anthony van Hoboken in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: 16. X. (Mit Vrieslander).Diary Oct 16: “From 5 to 6:30, Hoboken and Vrieslander; I give Hoboken all sorts of things I collected for him and broach the question of Oppel.”

20. Erster Blick auf die Händel-Suite, ½6h fort. Uebergebe ihm Leonore (?).Probably the book by Josef Braunstein, Beethoven und seine Leonore-Ouvertüren: eine historisch-stilkritische Untersuchung (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel,1927). – The parenthetic question-mark is in Jeanette Schenker’s hand.
23. Fingersatz u. Vortrag zu T. 1–8.

26. Bringt den 1. Satz in 16tel Notierung, die Einteilung der Ornamente, Triller usw. eingetragen; ich zeige die Sommernachtstraum-Ouvertüre (s. Albersheim);Diary Oct 23: “I work on the Overture to “A Midsummer Night's Dream,” for Albersheim, on Handel for Hoboken.” – Cf. Albersheim lesson notes for October 26. spreche von einer eventuell herauszugebenden Urlinie-Sammlung als Nachtrag zu den Beispielen des Freien Satzes, von einer möglichen Angliederung dieser Sammlung an das Archiv, falls der
Druck nicht zustande käme.Diary Oct 26: an extended discussion, beginning: “I sensed an opportunity to broach my plan concerning Urlinie manuscripts to Hoboken; I added that nothing is yet current, and that therefore a reply from him is not necessary. [...]”

30. Fingersatz bis zum Ende der Einleitung. Hausabend für den 7. XI. angesetzt, will an Oppel telegrafiren.Diary Oct 30: “Hoboken invites us for November 7, will also telegraph Oppel and invite him; I let slip a remark about the possibility of an Urlinie edition of the Chopin Etudes – he says nothing. I say, with the Russians, ‘nichevo.’”

6. Ueber Tuben u. Hörner; neu Chopin Etude op. 25V Gism als Terzenübung.Diary Nov 6: “Hoboken brings Dunn's little book on ornamentation; he asks if I should like to be present at the inauguration of the Archive; I explain why I am declining.” – John Petrie Dunn, Ornamentation in the Works of Chopin (London: Novello, 1921).

9. Literatur zur Terzen-Technik: Busoni in seiner Ausgabe des Wohltemperierten Klaviers, Galston Studienbuch,Gottfried Galston, Studienbuch (Berlin: Cassirer, 1910); a copy of this edition existed in Schenker’s diary at the time of his death. Schumann Vorwort zu op. 3.Studies for the Pianoforte, after Caprices of Paganini, Op. 3 (1832). Schumann’s foreword gives comprehensive instructions on the fingering of thirds in one hand (diatonic and chromatic scales), especially in preparation for Op. 3, No. 4, in B major. Etude Gism Fingersatz genau erläutert u. vermerkt; neu Etude op. 10II zum Vergleich des Fingersatzes. Bermerkungen zu Dunns Ornamentik.John Petrie Dunn, Ornamentation in the Works of Chopin (London: Novello, 1921).

13. Ueber Cubes Vorträge in Köln.In a letter of November 7 (OC 9/34, [5]), Felix-Eberhard von Cube reported that his series of lectures on Schenker’s theories at the Cologne Conservatory were going well. Er: „Nicht wahr, Vrieslander ist starr, alt geworden?“Diary Nov 13: “[...] Strangely, he initiated the conversation with the question: ‘Do you not find Vrieslander stiff and old?’ I could not think of any answer but this: ‘If a man of such energy succeeds in obtaining no proper employment, that will take its toll on him!’” – Probably Alexander Berrsche, Ein Gespräch zum Schubert-Gedenktag, Der Kunstwart (November 1928), a copy of which is preserved in the Schenker’s Scrapbook (OC 2). Etude
Gism, Linie. Ueber Schubert Hm-Sinfonie u. Berrsche im Kunstwart. Ich zeige die weiteren Parallelismen des 1. Terzzuges.
16. Etude Gism verglichen mit der Handschrift; er spielt das 1. Stück Händel.

23. Ohne Noten! Ich zeige den Brief von Berrsche, die Pedal-Studie von Rosenthal in seiner Liszt-Ausgabe.Diary Nov 23: “Hoboken appears, announces a trip to London (December 4–16) [...] I show him the letter from Berrsche, and Rosenthal's pedal study.” Der übrige Stoff aus dem Privaten, sogar zur Politik.

30. Mit Vrieslander! Ueber Vrieslanders Vortrag der Bdur-Sonate aus Anlaß seines Schubert-VortragsDiary Nov 28:” I go to hear Vrieslander's lecture. [Published as Das Organische in Schuberts ‘Himmlischer Länge,' Bericht über den internationalen Kongress für Schubertforschung, Wien 25. bis 29. November 1928 (Augsburg: Bennor Filser, 1929), pp. 220‒31.] [...] I arrive just in time as Vrieslander takes the podium. In terms of verbal and conceptual organization, the lecture reached a considerable elevation. The question that Vrieslander posed cannot, however, be answered without a [theoretical] background; thus he had to stumble about on the surface. He expressly rejected the viewpoint of the Urlinie and all that immediately follows from it, without realizing that, precisely in so doing, he was taking himself along a false path. But whatever mistakes he may have made, his way of looking at things clearly towers over all objective statements of today's musicians. A high wind is blowing there, and it brings other results to the cause, even to the language, than one is accustomed to hearing on such occasions – his performance at the piano, however, stood well below the level of his theoretical discussion: a veritably unenjoyable rubato, aggravated by over-accentuations that found no equilibrium, proved disconcerting. One could observe that he is a good player, but one reacted against his performance.” u. über die Replik von Dr. Koeltzsch.Hans Koeltzsch (Költzsch) (1901–81), German musicologist and critic, author of Franz Schubert in seinen Klaviersonaten (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1927). Ich zeige die Skizzen zur VI. Sinfonie u. erläutere sie.Diary Nov 30: “At 5:30, Hoboken and Vrieslander: they bring the book by Költzsch (belonging to Deutsch); we speak about the performance of the Sonata in B major, about the lack of equilibrium; [...] I show them the sketches for Beethoven's Sixth Symphony.”
18. XII. Wieder eingetroffen; allerhand Besprechungen.

21. Er spielt die Etude Gism bis zum a2-Teil, die Am-Etude zuende, die Linie zeige ich ihm. Er bringt den Erst-
-druck des Schubert-Menuetts; wiederholt Händel 1. Satz, erster Einblick in den 2. Satz.
28. Wiederholt auch Chopins Etude Fm u. Fdur u. Händel Allegro 1. Teil; ich erläutere 16tel um 16tel .

4. I. Fingersatz zum Allegro ganz. Ich zeige Schubert Cdur-Sinfonie, Andante, Fdur-Stelle. Er möchte Bruckner u. Mahler kennen lernen u. zu diesem Zwecke vierhändig durchspielen; ich erkläre mich dazu bereit.

8. Ich lese den für den Kunstwart bestimmten Aufsatz vor.Eine Rettung der klassischen Musik-Texte: Das Archiv für Photogramme in der National-Bibliothek, Wien (Widmung Anthony van Hoboken), Der Kunstwart, vol. 42, No. 6 (March 1929), 359–67. Bruckner I vierhändig; dazu aus Bruckner IV Ländler.Most probably the Trio section of the third movement, in ¾ time and marked “Nicht zu schnell” (not too fast) and, in smaller type “keinesfalls schleppend” (in no way dragging).

11. Er kommt auf die im Aufsatz gemachte Unterscheidung von Mutter- u. Vatersprache zurück; ich erläutere diese mit historischen u.
theoretischen Gründen. Neu: Chopin op. XXII, Analyse u. Handschrift.Diary Jan 5: “I work on Chopin's Op. 10 No. 12 (for Hoboken).” Mahler II. Sinfonie, 1. Satz flüchtig. v. H. erklärt sich bereit, den Freien Satz zu übernehmen (!!). Bruckner I v. H. primo, 3. Satz. Zum Schluß zahlt er endlich!
18. Bruckner letzter Satz.

22. Bruckner III, 1. Satz bis zur Durchführung. Beginne in Em. Bach den Abschnitt vom Vortrag.C. P. E. Bach, Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Eng. transl. William J. Mitchell (New York: W. W. Norton; London: Cassell, 1949; London: Eulenburg, 1974), pp. 366–79 “Performance” (= chapter XXXI).

29. Ueber drei Stellen in Vrieslanders Revision des Scherzo von Chopin.Diary Feb 19: “I show Hoboken the corrections to Vrieslander's work.” – Cf. diary Sept 30, 1929: “At present, only a single article is ready for publication, the one by Vrieslander on Chopin's Op. 54“ – designated for the planned but never realized Mitteilungen of the Photogramm Archive; perhaps ultimately published as Otto Vrieslander: Eine Stelle aus Chopins Scherzo op. 54, Der Dreiklang Heft 8/9 (1937/38), 208–11. Ueber die Frage der Revision im fotografischen Archiv, über meine Monografie zur Eroica;Schenker’s analysis of Beethoven’s “Eroica” Symphony, at this stage envisioned as a monograph, was ultimately published as Beethovens Dritte Sinfonie zum erstenmal in ihrem wahren Inhalt dargestellt, Das Meisterwerk in der Musik III (1930), 29–101 and app. (Eng. transl., vol. III, pp. 10–68 and 81–115). er erklärt sich bereit, die Abschrift zu machen. Ueber den Freien Satz: empfiehlt zu stechen, nicht zu fotografiren, erzählt, Mandyczewski habe sich wegen der III. Sinfonie von Haydn an ihm
gewendet.Most probably Haydn’s Symphony in E major, Hob. I:99. Prior to Eusebius Mandyczewski’s numbering of the Haydn symphonies from 1 to 104, which Hoboken adopted in his thematic catalogue, the last and most famous symphonies were assigned the lowest numbers, e.g. the “Drumroll” Symphony was No. 1, the “London” Symphony (in D major) was No. 2. At this time, today’s No. 99 was commonly known as “Symphony No. 3.” In this earlier sequence, the symphony in D major known today as No. 86 was identified as “Symphony No. 10”: see Hoboken’s lesson notes for April 5, 1929. Die Apotheker Oesterreichs lassen im Archiv die Partitur von Haydn „Der Apotheker“ facsimiliren als Geschenk an die Amerikanischen Apotheker!
1. II. Bringt einen eigenen Marsch, vierhändig – treffliche Anlage; zeigt auch Streichquartett, Ouvertüre.Diary Feb 1: “Hoboken brings his march and two earlier compositions.”
5. Improvisire einige Korrekturen zum Marsch. Bruckner III, 1. Satz zuende.
6. Bei uns zu Abend.
8. Zeige weitere Korrekturen zum Marsch. Etude 10XII fortgesetzt u. gespielt.

12. Vortrag von Emanuel Bach fortgesetzt,Presumably C. P. E. Bach, Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Eng. transl. William J. Mitchell (New York: W. W. Norton; London: Cassell, 1949; London: Eulenburg, 1974), pp. 366–79 “Performance” (= chapter XXXI). ich spiele aus Em. Bach., IV. Heft für Kenner u. Liebhaber vor: Rondo in Bd u. Ed, zwei Fantasien – als Beleg zu einigen Paragraphen des Vortrags. Dann Bruckner, v. H. primo, einige Stellen erläutert.

15. Erste
Korrektur des vierhändigen Marsches. Besprechung.Diary Feb 15: “Hoboken brings a second march; we talk through it.”

19. Zweite Korrektur mit Zugrundelegung meiner Vorschläge bis zum Trio.This refers to a march by Hoboken for piano four-hands. Es fällt das Wort: „Ich kenne alle Städte nur Berlin kenne ich noch nicht!“

22. Ich übergebe das Manuscript von Vrieslander;Presumably Vrieslander’s article on the revision of Chopin’s Scherzo in E major, Op. 54, mentioned in Hoboken’s lesson notes for January 29, on which Schenker has been working since then. It was intended for a volume of the planned, but never realized, Mitteilungen of the Photogram Archive. korrigire das Trio des Marsches,Diary Feb 20: “Continuation of the corrections for Hoboken." er nimmt mein Blatt zu sich. Etude 10XII zuende. Die Mitteilungen beschlossen. Bruckner Adagio. Plan für das nächste Jahr beschlossen, darunter ein Heftchen von 6 Märschen.

26. Bruckner III Adagio, Scherzo, Finale mit Erklärungen. Zum Beschluß Mozart-Variationen Gdur vierhändig gespielt.Most probably the Andante and Variations in G major, K. 501 – An undated sketch in Schenker’s hand for a graph of the third movement, Scherzo, of Bruckner’s Third Symphony survives at OC 38/37, labelled “Gegenb[ei]sp[iel]” (“counter-example”): at this time Schenker’s collecting of compositions that lacked the coherence of Urlinie and Ursatz focussed on Reger, Bruckner, and Hindemith.

1. III Das Bild des 3. Händel-Stückes gebracht, ich korrigire. Er zeigt Raubdrucke
von E. Bach über Klopstock.Diary March 1: “I give Hoboken the article, show him Vrieslander's letter, and ask him once again for the revision work. He says that agents are no longer so willing to work for him as before, and adds: ‘I shall pay 10% more, if I really want these pieces; for I should gladly round off the collection so that I can get on to something else.’ (!) Moreover, he is very hard-working.” – The article in question was: Heinrich Schenker, Eine Rettung der klassischen Musik-Texte: Das Archiv für Photogramme in der National-Bibliothek, Wien (Widmung Anthony van Hoboken), in Der Kunstwart, No. 6, March 1929, 42nd year, 359–67. The pieces are presumably Hoboken’s six marches.
5. Ich gehe v. H. Bild des Allegro durch.

8. Spielt op. 10II u. 10XII u. 25V. Im Bild des Allegro, 2. Teil erläutert u. befestigt; Fragen zum Text aus dem 1. Teil bereingt. Spielt das Allegro zum erstenmal, Vortrag eingezeichnet. 1. Stück wiederholt.

12. Wegen Verletzung des Fingers Pause im Spiel.Diary Feb 12: “Hoboken cannot play, on account of a finger injury, thus gets too far with Handel, already getting beyond the Fugue.” Neu: Händel Fuge; ich zeige an eigenen Bildern wie zu verfahren sei.

15. Zu Casals Vortrag der Brahms Sonate op. 99 u. der Bach Suite Dm.The concert on March 11, 1929 in the large hall of the Vienna Konzerthaus, Pablo Casals with Otto Schulhof, piano, program: Brahms, Cello Sonata in F major; Bach Cello Suite in D minor; Fauré, Sicilienne; Rimsky-Korsakov, Vol du Bourdon; Cassado, Folies; Saint-Saens, Appassionata; Locatelli, Sonata. – Schenker attended and recorded in his diary for March 12, 1929: “Casals concert: in every respect a beautiful program; he plays Brahms's Sonata in F major: the first two movements were less convincing, however the third and fourth movements proceeded with absolute perfection; Bach's Suite in D minor was equally convincing, the details as ever outstanding.” Zeige den 1. u. 2. Satz aus Mozart Sinfonie Esdur. Bruckner III, Finale. Zeige die Unmöglichkeit der Stimmführung. Zum Schluß: verweist mich auf den Verlag Filser!! Brahms op. 117 Handschrift, einige Bermerkungen dazu.

19. Zum Vortrag
der Jupiter-Sinfonie u. Brahms IV. (Furtwängler).The seventh Philharmonic subscription concert, in the great hall of the Musikverein Building on March 17, 1929, the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra under Wilhelm Furtwängler. Schenker attended and recorded in his diary: “At 11 o'clock, walked to the concert. Conversation with Weisse, he says of Furtwängler: ‘and yet only a performer concerned with the foreground and effects.’ The first movement of the ‘Jupiter’ Symphony was pale; other shortcomings arise from insufficient knowledge of the score, especially in the Andante. A piece by Ernst Bloch – apparently a Zionist who, however, writes bad music. In Brahms's Fourth Symphony, much that is attractive – most of it, however, was unsatisfactory.” v. H. trägt nach, Filser sei Antisemit, ich könne auf ihm nicht rechnen!

22. Fingersatz zu Händels III. Stück, Ausführung der Verzierungen; zeige Händel XIII Suite Bdur; Notierung der Triolen in früheren Zeiten. Haas u. die Mitteilungen; Haas empfiehlt ein ungedrucktes Mendelssohn-Stück.
26. Ich zeige Hässler.Probably his Three Easy Sonatas, published in 1928 as No. 20 of Nagel’s Musikarchiv; Schenker received a copy of it several days before (diary entry, March 16).
2. IV. Ueber den Vrieslander-Zwischenfall (30%). Ueber Judas Maccabäus; Haydn „Die sieben Worte“; Jupiter-Sinfonie; Vergleich mit der Handschrift.

5. Zum Furtwängler Konzert: Haydn Sinfonie Ddur No 10 vierhändig. Zu Vrieslander: „Ich würde krank werden, wenn ich die Rente fortzahlen müßte“ (!!) „Mit den
30% hat Vrieslander Recht“ – „Kann Vrieslander die Arbeit nicht in 14 Tagen vollenden, so daß er noch vor den Ferien fertig wird?“ (!)There is a long discussion of the Vrieslander matter in the diary for February 5.

9. Ich lehne die Mitteilungen ab.Mitteilungen: a planned periodical reporting the research of the Photogram Archive, which was never realized. – Diary Feb 9: “In front of Hoboken, I decline [co-editing] the Communications: Vrieslander is a lost cause for us, Albersheim is getting married, the two of us cannot take this on ourselves, alone.” Zur Revision gehört ein Stab von Musikern – „Das kann ich nicht“ sagt v. H. Ich: Einmalig dürfen die Mitteilungen nicht sein. Korrigire v. H. Bilder zur Händel-Fuge; lasse mir vom Furtwängler-Konzert erzählen.The eighth subscription concert of the Vienna Philharmonic, conducted by Furtwängler, which Schenker attended earlier that day and which included Haydn’s Symphony in D, Hob. I:86, and Beethoven’s Eroica. – Längere Unterrichtspause.

21. V. Ueber Toscanini in Lucia; über die Unmöglichkeit der Rettung eines solchen Werkes. Toscaninis Verdienst in Ehren – sicher die erste Ausführung, der die Kraft eignet, jene ältere Musik zu erneuern, wenn nicht bedeutende Mängel dem entgegenstünden:
Der Baß verleugnet die Gesetze eines kontrapunktischen Außensatzes, in allen Gliedern der Musik steckt das Kontrapunktische seit Beginn der Kunst im Abendland. Nach dem flüchtigen Augenblick der Monodie ist die Musik zum Kontrapunkt ein Außensatz zurückgekehrt. Ein Leere im Außensatz durch mangelhaftes Durchkomponieren des Basses rächt sich, s. Gluck, die italienischen Opern, französische, unter den Italienern nur Scarlatti ein wahrer Komponist. Ueber den Unterschied von Rhythmik u. Metrik – Begriffwerdung nur in Rahmen des Kontrapunkts möglich: Rhythmik ist ein kontrapunktisches Ereignis, Metrik ein absolutes, daher z.B. im Jazz, der italienischen, französischen
Oper noch kein Rhythmus – in diesen Fällen ist das Wort Rhythmus eine Falschmeldung, wie auch in dem Begriff Technik, in dem die Allgemeinheit nicht die wahre Technik des Vortrags versteht, wie sie den Meistern eigen ist, sondern eine vom schlichten Lesen u. schlechtem Spiel abgezogene Klaviertechnik. – Ueber Harburgers Aufsatz;Diary Feb 5: Hoboken brings articles by Harburger.” – Diary June 7: “[Hoboken] gives me an essay by Harburger, on behalf of the author.” – He gave Schenker two more Harburger articles on July 11, having brought him several on February 5. seine Unsicherheit kommt daher, weil die Auskomponierung als Um u. Auf der Musik noch nicht in seinem Instinkt u. Blickfeld ist. – Ueber Veröffentlichungen des Archives. Habe selbst keine Zeit, Vrieslanders Manuscript zu lesen, überlasse es mir – trotzdem ich ablehne!

24. Vrieslanders Revision zu Chopin
Etude Cm durchgearbeitet.Previously mentioned in Hoboken’s lesson notes for January 29 and February 22. v. H. läßt sein Manuscript über den Sommer bei mir zurück, bringt Originalstimmen zur EroicaDiary May 24: “Hoboken brings the original parts for the Third Symphony; he is leaving his manuscripts with me over the summer.” u. die Originalausgabe von Chopin op. 10II.
28. Korrektur des Fugenbildes abgeschlossen, Fingersatz eingetragen.

31. Ueber den Drei Masken Verlag u. den bisherigen Vertrag zum Jahrbuch. Ich zeige einiges aus den Stimmen der revidirten III. Sinfonie, auch die Ausführung der Fermate zur E. Bach Sonate nach Bildern des Frl. Elias, in Zusammenhang damit meine Kadenz zur Esdur Sonate. Zeige Schrenk’s Aufsatz über die Auferstehung der Meister.Probably an article by Walter Schrenk (1893–1932) in the Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, for which he was a music critic from 1920 until his untimely death in a traffic accident. – Elias’s elaborated fermatas of a C. P. E. Bach sonata, in her own hand with emendations by Schenker, are preserved at OC 15/7–8 and graphed at OC 15/9. Schenker’s elaboration of a fermata of a C. P. E. Bach Fantasia in E major is preserved as OC 15/12–13, and his graph of the cadenza to the latter work is preserved at OC 15/11. (OC 15/3–13 all concern works by C. P. E. Bach.

4. VI. Em. Bach Vortrag zuende.Presumably C. P. E. Bach, Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Eng. transl. William J. Mitchell (New York: W. W. Norton; London: Cassell, 1949; London: Eulenburg, 1974), pp. 366–79 “Performance” (= chapter XXXI). Aus Brahms-Haydn-Variationen einige Fragen die Intervalle betreffend u. 5–5-Folgen. Zeige die Rhapsodie
Hmoll, über die Bedeutung von für die Synthese. Ueber diagram: wholenote rest on 5-line staff = die Stelle im letzten Satz op. 81a: eine psychologische Verbindung.

5. Kuratoriumssitzung bei v. H. Ich lehne einmalige Mitteilungen ab, Haas stimmt zu.Diary June 5: “4:30 at Hoboken's, meeting with Haas and Kromer. Hoboken trips me up by asking my opinion about the Communications. I give a real speech, which I succeed in delivering fluently. Haas agrees in every respect with me: I say no!”

7. Ziehe meine Gedanken über die Mitteilungen nach. Zeige Chopin Sonate Bmoll, Finale; S. Bach Generalbaß fortgesetzt. Letzter Abschnitt: Erleichterungen.J. S. Bach, Vorschriften und Grundsätze zum vierstimmigen Spielen des General-Bass oder Accompagnement (c. 1738). A facsimile and English translation of this manuscript was published as Precepts and Principles for Playing the Thorough-Bass or Accompanying in Four Parts, Eng. transl. Pamela Poulin (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994). Schenker often referred to this work and Bach’s Generalbassbüchlein

11. Abschiedsbesuch mit der Frau.Diary June 11: “Hoboken does not arrive for his lesson until 6 o'clock, what’s more with his wife; they stay for half an hour. I specifically return to the question of the Communications and explain that these and the Archive are separate concepts. Hoboken can rest on the laurels of the Archive even without Communications.”

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Anthony van Hoboken in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: October 16: (with Vrieslander).
October 20: First look at the Handel suite, he leaves at 5:30. I give him Leonore (?).
October 23: Fingering and performance for bars 1–8.

October 26: He brings the first movement in 16th-note notation, having entered the distribution of the ornaments, trills, etc. I show him the Overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream (cf. Albersheim); I speak of the possibility of publishing a collection of Urlinie graphs as a supplement to the examples in Free Composition, of possibly incorporating this collection into the Archive in the event that the
publication did not materialize.
October 30: Fingering up to the end of the Introduction. Evening get-together arranged for November 7; he will send Oppel a telegram.
November 2: A look back at the Sarabande from J. S. Bach’s Suite in E major; he enters the ornaments very precisely here, too.
November 6: Concerning tubas and horns; Chopin Etude Op. 25, No. 5, in G minor, new, as an exercise in thirds.

November 9: Literature on the technique of playing in thirds: Busoni in his edition of The Well-Tempered Clavier, Galston’s Studienbuch, Schumann’s foreword to his Op. 3. Etude in G minor, fingering precisely elucidated and noted down. Etude Op. 10, No. 2, new, for the purpose of comparing fingering. Remarks on Dunn’s Ornamentation.

November 13: On Cube’s lectures in Cologne. He: “Is it not true that Vrieslander has become stiff, old?” Etude
in G minor, voice-leading line. On Schubert’s B minor Symphony and Berrsche’s article in Der Kunstwart. I show him the further parallelisms of the first third-progression.
November 16: Etude in G minor compared with the manuscript; he plays the first movement of Handel.
November 23: Without music! I show him Berrsche’s letter, Rosenthal’s pedal study in his edition of Liszt. The remaining material from private matters, even on politics.

November 30: With Vrieslander! On Vrieslander’s performance of the B major Sonata on the occasion of his Schubert lecture, and on Dr. Koeltzsch’s reply. I show him the sketches for the Sixth Symphony and elucidate them.
December 18: He has arrived again; all sorts of discussions.

December 21: He plays the Etude in G minor as far as the a2 section, the A minor Etude to the end; I show him the voice-leading line. He brings the
first edition of the Schubert minuet; repeats the first movement of Handel; first glimpse of the second movement.
December 28: He also revisits Chopin's Etudes in F minor and F major and the first part of Handel’s Allegro; I elucidate it one sixteenth note after another.

January 4: Fingering for the entire Allegro. I show him the F major passage in the Andante of Schubert’s C major Symphony. He would like to get to know Bruckner and Mahler, and for this purpose to play through their works four-hands; I declare myself ready for this.
January 8: I read to him the article intended for Der Kunstwart. Bruckner’s First Symphony, four-hands; in addition, the Ländler from Bruckner’s Fourth.

January 11: He returns to the distinction made in my article between “mother tongue” and “father tongue”; I elucidate it with historical and
theoretical arguments. New: Chopin Op. 10, No. 12, analysis and manuscript. Mahler’s Second Symphony, first movement hastily. Hoboken declares that he is prepared to bear the production costs of Free Composition (!!). Bruckner’s First Symphony, third movement, Hoboken on the upper part. At the end, he finally pays!
January 18: Last movement of the Bruckner.
January 22: Bruckner’s Third Symphony, first movement as far as the development section. I begin the section “Performance” in C. P. E. Bach.

January 29: Concerning three places in Vrieslander’s revision of Chopin’s Scherzo. On the matter of revision in the Photogram Archive, on my monograph on the Eroica; he declares himself prepared to make the fair copy. Concerning Free Composition: he recommends engraving, not photography, says that Mandyczewski approached him with regard to Haydn’s Third Symphony.
The apothecaries of Austria will have a facsimile of the score of Haydn’s Der Apotheker placed in the Archive, as a gift to the American apothecaries!
February 1: He brings a march of his own composition, for piano four-hands: splendid construction; he also shows me a string quartet and an overture.
February 5: I improvise a few corrections for the March. Bruckner’s Third Symphony, first movement played to the end.
February 6: At our place in the evening!
February 8: I show him further corrections for his march. Etude Op. 10, No. 12 continued and played.

February 12: “Performance” by C. P. E. Bach continued, I play the Rondos in B major and E major and two fantasies from C. P. E. Bach’s fourth volume of Sonatas … for Connoisseurs and Amateurs – as support for a few paragraphs from “Performance.” Then Bruckner, Hoboken on the upper part, a few passages elucidated.

February 15: First
correction of his march for piano four hands. Discussion.
February 19: Second correction, with justification of my recommendations, as far as the Trio. He drops the remarks: “I know every city; only Berlin I do not yet know!”

February 22: I give him Vrieslander’s manuscript; I correct the Trio of his march, he takes my sheet with him. Etude Op. 10, No. 12 completed. The Communications of the Photogram Archive decided on. Bruckner Adagio. Plan for the following year decided on, including a little book of six marches.
February 26: Bruckner's Third Symphony: Adagio, Scherzo, and finale with clarifications. At the end, Mozart’s Variations in G major played four-hands.

March 1: The graph of the third movement of the Handel piece brought; I correct it. He shows me pirate editions
from C. P. E. Bach; to Klopstock.[30]
March 5: I go through Hoboken’s graph of the Allegro.

March 8: He plays Op. 10, No. 2, Op. 10, No. 12, and Op. 25, No. 5. In the graph of the Allegro, the second part elucidated and confirmed; questions about the text of the first part cleared up. He plays the Allegro for the first time, the performance markings written into the score. The first movement repeated.
March 12: On account of an injury to his finger, a pause in his playing. New: Handel Fugue: I show him how to proceed, using my own graphs.

March 15: On Casals’s performances of Brahms’s Sonata Op. 99 and Bach’s D minor Suite. I show him the first and second movements of Mozart’s Symphony in E major. Bruckner’s Third Symphony, finale. I show him the impossibility of the voice-leading. At the end: he refers me to the publishing house of Filser!! Brahms Op. 117, manuscript, a few observations on it.

March 19:On the performance
of the “Jupiter” Symphony and Brahms’s Fourth Symphony (Furtwängler). Hoboken adds that Filser is an antisemite, and that I could not count on him!

March 22: Fingering for the third movement of Handel, realization of the ornaments; I show him Handel’s Suite No. 13 in B major; the notation of triplets in earlier times. Haas and the Communications of the Photogram Archive; Haas recommends an unpublished piece by Mendelssohn.
March 26: I show him Hässler.
April 2: Concerning the Vrieslander contretemps (30%). On Judas Maccabeus; Haydn’s The Seven Last Words; “Jupiter” Symphony; comparison with the autograph manuscript.

April 5: On Furtwängler’s concert: Haydn Symphony No. 10 in D major, played four-hands. On Vrieslander: “I would become ill if I had to continue paying his annuity” (!!) “With his
30%, Vrieslander is right” – “Can Vrieslander not complete the work in two weeks, so that he will be finished before the holidays?” (!)

April 9: I decline co-editing the Communications. The editing should be done by a staff of musicians – “That is something I cannot do,” says Hoboken. I: “The Communications ought not to appear just once. I correct Hoboken’s graphs for the Handel Fugue; I allow myself to talk about Furtwängler’s concert. – A lengthy break in the tuition.

May 21: Concerning Toscanini in Lucia; on the impossibility of rescuing such a work.. Toscanini’s merit of honor – for sure the first performance to which his powers are suited to renew this older music, were it not that its significant shortcomings stood in his way:
the bass line repudiates the laws of a contrapuntal outer-voice structure. The contrapuntal element has been a fixture in all branches of music, since the beginnings of the artform in the West. After a fleeting moment of monody, music has returned to a contrapuntal outer-voice design. An emptiness in this outer-voice construction, as a result of a faulty through-composition, will take its toll, as it did in Gluck, Italian opera, French opera; among the Italians, only Scarlatti is a true composer. On the difference between rhythm and metre – they become concepts only in a framework of counterpoint: rhythm is a contrapuntal phenomenon, metre an absolute one. Thus for example in jazz, in Italian and French
opera, there is as yet no rhythm; in these instances the word “rhythm” is a false concept, as is also that of “technique,” in which ordinary people do not understand the true technique of performance, as it appertains to the masters, but rather a piano technique derived from mechanical reading and bad playing. – On Harburger’s essay; his insecurity is the result of composing-out, the alpha and omega of music, not yet being in his instincts and field of vision. – Concerning the publications of the Archive. I myself have no time in which to read Vrieslander’s manuscript: leave it with me – despite my having declined!

May 24: Vrieslander’s revision of his article on Chopin
Etude in C minor gone through thoroughly. Hoboken is leaving his manuscript with me over the summer; he brings the original parts to the "Eroica" and the original edition of Chopin’s Op. 10, No.2
May 28: Correction to the graphs of the Fugue completed, fingering entered.

May 31: Concerning Drei Masken Verlag and the contract for the Yearbook until now. I show him something from the parts of the revised Third Symphony; also the realization of the fermatas in C. P. E. Bach’s sonata based on Miss Elias’s graphs and, in this connection, my cadenza for the Sonata in E. I show him Schrenk’s essay on the resurrection of the Masters.

June 4: C. P. E. Bach’s chapter “Performance” finished. From Brahms’s Haydn Variations, some questions concerning the intervals and parallel fifths. I show him the Rhapsody
in B minor, concerning the significance of for the synthesis. On diagram: wholenote rest on 5-line staff = the place in the last movement of Op. 81a: a psychological connection.
June 5: Board of Trustees meeting at Hoboken’s place. I reject one-off Communications, Haas agrees.
June 7: I recapitulate my thoughts about the Communications. I show him the finale of Chopin’s Sonata in B minor; J. S. Bach’s thoroughbass continued. Last section: Simplifications.
June 11: Farewell visit, with his wife.

20. Wiederholt Esd, Hd, dazu Fisd, Hd, Asd.
3. XI. Träumerei, Nocturne Gd, Cm, Fm, Ed.

17. Wiederholung vom 3. XI, dazu Berçeuse u. Prélude Desd.Diary Nov 17, an extraordinary protracted outburst begins: “Miss Kahn unexpectedly gives me cause for resistance, especially in the repeat of Träumerei, which she requested for a pupil of hers. I lost my patience; I saw myself confronted by the failure of my personal kindness, my pedagogical effort, to produce any results after more than twenty years. [...]”
1. XII. Wiederholt Etude 10I u. 10III; Walzer Asd, Cism, Desd.Diary Feb 2, 1929: “I set matters straight with Miss Kahn; I scream vehemently, she cries.”

15. op. 10 zuende.Cf. Diary Feb 16: “In bars 1 and 2 of the Sonata Op. 111, Miss Kahn, after many years of struggling, presents the correct relationship between the sforzandi, in the way that I wish; and instead of apologizing for taking such a long time compared to all my other pupils, she says with a downright infernal innocence: ‘Do you know what was wrong? The right hand: I had held it down too long.’”

5. I. op. 25
bis No 11.
19. op. 109 ganz, op. 110, 1. Satz.
2. II. op. 110 zuende, gut; Chopin Ballade Gm – wie neu! op. 111, Anfang. „Ich kann so nicht spielen.“!
16. Für Frau Greger Träumerei, Impromptu CmProbably the Impromptu in C minor, Op. 66. u. ein Stück von Dwořak; op. 111 zuende.
2. III. Ballade Gm wiederholt; Chopin Sonate Bm – wie neu!
16. op. 101 wiederholt; neu Chopin Préludes 1, 2, 3. Einiges von Chopin wiederholt.

6. IV. Polonaise Asd wiederholt; Prélude No 4 bis Ed.That is, all the preludes from No. 4, which is in E minor, to No. 9 in E major.; vierhändig zum erstenmal: Haydn Sinfonie No 11,In older numberings of the Haydn symphonies, the more famous works were given low numbers. “Symphony No. 11” was almost certainly No. 100 in G major (“Military”). ersten u. letzten Satz.

20. Beethoven op. 2I;Diary April 20: “Miss Kahn plays Op. 2, No. 1, and, after being rebuked about the performance of the Finale, observes that in the first issue of Der Tonwille I gave precisely the instruction that I now reject! With a wickedness that is given only to sick persons, she adds: ‘I am not offering any criticisms of you; I have read carefully, and if you reread it too, then you will find the instruction that one should hardly touch the notes.’” Prélude bis Gism.That is, a continuation of the sequence of Chopin preludes from the previous lesson (which had stopped at No. 9 in E major) as far as No. 12 in G minor.

4. V. Beethoven op. 10III.Diary May 4: “From 9:30, work on the preludes for Miss Kahn. — Miss Kahn does not apologize; she behaves as if she had done nothing improper during the previous lesson. – But Miss Elias has said, in the meantime, that she [Miss Kahn] misread [the Tonwille text]. This desire to brush things aside, without apologizing, bothers me greatly; and so I explain my principles about performance, tolerating no individuality on the part of my pupils in my studio. She cries; she does not remember, because she does not want to remember, even comes back to her ‘better method,’ but in the end plays as I would like.”
18. Klavierkonzert Esd.Probably Beethoven’s Fifth Piano Concerto, rather than one of the three Mozart concertos in the key of E.

1. VI. Préludes bis 12–16; Sonate Dd 1. u. 2. Satz wiederholt.Diary June 1: “Miss Kahn is sad, feels ashamed, and attempts to apologize. I say: ‘You have made a martyr of me’ – she claims not to know anything about that.”

15. VI. Préludes fortgesetzt u. abgeschlossen.Diary June 15: “Miss Kahn brings roses; I arrange a further lesson with her, next Saturday.” – Lesson notes for June 15 and 22 are written as a single entry.
22. Préludes fortgesetzt u. abgeschlossen.Lesson notes for June 15 and 22 are written as a single entry.

as far as No. 11.
